<div class="blue">ILLEGAL ACTIVITY

Tracking illegal activity is crucial for policy relevance. This is particularly true for violent crime, which is typically the focus of criminal-legal policy and public concern. Importantly, self-reported criminal activity is a far more sensitive measure of behavioral change than arrest records alone, given that individuals are generally arrested for only a fraction of crimes committed (< 1 in 10). Furthermore, capturing the type and frequency of criminal activity is critical for economic evaluations, as there is wide variation in the extent to which different types of crime lead to an arrest, conviction, incarceration, and costs to the victims.  Combined, these costs are often orders of magnitude higher than those associated with healthcare resource utilization. Thus, including these measures greatly increases the likelihood of demonstrating economic value for interventions that effectively reduce criminal activity.

Field Label:
<div class="blue">Health-Related Quality of Life (PROPr)

Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is recommended as a core measure of recovery by the National Academy of Sciences, and is highly prioritized by individuals with lived experience of SUD.  Of particular importance is a comprehensive HRQoL measure that extends beyond basic physical health.  The PROPr is comprised of PROMIS measures, which were developed through a major NIH initiative to provide standardized assessments of functioning over eight essential domains (anxiety, cognitive functioning, depression, fatigue, sleep, pain, physical functioning, social functioning).  The PROPr also produces a preference-based composite score used to calculate quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) -- the gold standard for cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA), and a core metric recommended by NIH to harmonize with existing HEAL- and NIDA-funded studies.

Section Header: Quality of life is an important part of recovery.  This section asks about eight key areas of well-being, including mood, thinking, sleep, pain, physical functioning, and social functioning, to provide a more complete picture of your health.
